sections.html:
• Name: Blue-Legged Hermit Crab
  • Other names: Dwarf Blue Hermit Crab, Equal-Handed Hermit Crab, Blue-leg Reef Hermit Crab
  • Scientific name: Clibanarius tricolor
  • Minimum tank size: 20 litres
  • Breeding: Very difficult
  • Water type: Saltwater, specific gravity (SG) 1.018–1.025
  • Optimal KH: 8–16
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: Omnivore/carnivore
  • Temperament: Semi-aggressive
  • Life span: up to 2 years
  • Colour form: Blue, black, orange

The Blue Leg Hermit Crab (Clibanarius tricolor) is a small marine invertebrate heavily exploited by the ornamental pet industry. Hermit crabs are unique among higher crustaceans (like shrimp, crabs or crayfish) because they generally utilize snail shells as portable shelters for protection because their body is soft and fragile.

Among hermit crabs, the Blue Legged Hermit Crab is highly valued both because of its aesthetic value and apparent ability to control the small sea anemone Aiptasia spp., considered a nuisance by aquarium hobbyists. In addition to their colorful appearance, they are low maintenance hermit crabs that are very hardy and require little care.

The Blue Leg Hermit Crab is certainly one of the most abundant and widespread small hermit crab species throughout the Caribbean Sea and western Atlantic.

They are very common in shallow waters (two meters or less) along open shores on both the north and south coast of Curaçao.
These hermit crabs form temporarily large aggregations during low tides in the intertidal zone where they find refuge in depressions beneath rocks on hard-bottoms.
They require a minimum tank size of 40 litres for a small group of 2–3 crabs. Ideally, to avoid crowding the aquarium, one should aim for just one Blue leg hermit crab per 11–15 litres of water.

The water should be between 22–26°C, with a pH between 8.0–8.5. The tank should also have a specific gravity of 1.020 to 1.025, and the hardness of the water should be between 8–16 °d. They can tolerate most types of water movement but prefer slow-moving water.

In general, they are not very picky creatures. If given time, they can adapt to a higher or lower temperature, salinity, and other water parameters.

For the substrate, you can use either sand or small gravel. In the wild, Blue leg hermit crabs usually prefer to live in intertidal sandy-bottom substrates. Therefore, sand is the most ideal substrate for them. These crabs are great at aiding in aerating the substrate as well.

Tip: If you are purchasing gravel, make sure that the grains are small enough for the hermit crab to sift.

Include plenty of live rock for the hermit crab to graze on, and the rock will also double as hiding areas that help to make it feel secure.

They do not need fancy filtration and lighting. You can just purchase a normal LED aquarium light.

Important: Before putting them in your tank do not forget to acclimate them.

These hermit crabs have become popular residents of aquariums because of their so-called "janitorial capabilities."

The Blue Leg Hermit Crab is an active omnivore and opportunistic in its feeding habits. They spend most of their time looking for food such as organic debris, decayed and fresh macro-algae, macroscopic pieces of dead and live animal tissues.

In the aquarium, they usually play the role of a clean-up crew. They will eat fish or shrimp food leftovers, fish wastes, leftover meaty food, dried seaweed, dead plants, many types of macroalgae including green hair algae and cyanobacteria and will sift the substrate for foodstuff. Because of their small size, they are able to reach some areas other tank janitors cannot reach.

Note: some aquarists consider their hermit crabs to be scavengers and do not feed them any additional food. This is true, they are scavengers. However, it is still advisable to provide the occasional treat, for example krill, Mysis, frozen carnivore cubes, pellets or flakes.

Aiptasia: Blue Leg Hermit Crabs have been reported eating Aiptasia. The problem is that if they can find something else to eat, they will always choose the tastier food over Aiptasia. Therefore, in tanks with lots of goodies and excess feeding, these crabs will tend to ignore Aiptasia.

According to experiments, in the wild, Blue Legged Hermit Crabs exhibit high site fidelity and do not make large daily movements, having an average home range no larger than 2 m in diameter.

This species is nocturnal. During the day, the crabs move about slowly or rest. Feeding activity begins at dusk and continues throughout the night.

Blue Leg Hermit Crabs are social and relatively peaceful animals. They usually congregate among detritus-covered rocks as a group. They prefer to stick to their own group, where they feel more comfortable and secure. In an experiment, biologists marked the shells of two different groups with red and blue ink and replaced them in their respective groups. Observations over the first few days revealed relative group stability: the majority (82%) of the marked crabs returned to their own group.

Clibanarius tricolor is neither a rapidly nor slowly moving crab relative to other species. Although surprisingly agile for an organism carrying so much extraneous weight, individuals often tumble over backwards when attempting to crawl over an obstacle and lose their hold on it. They are usually able to right themselves rapidly through movements of their second legs.

Blue Leg Hermit Crabs usually do not show any change in their behavior when they meet. One may crawl over the other or they may pass one another without any apparent notice. Even when one hermit crab starts making aggressive movements, the other frequently shows no change in behavior, unless attacked.

Shell-fighting behaviour

When two crabs come in contact, the most frequently used aggressive signal is the single raise of the legs (0.24 seconds). The ambulatory raise is executed with the limb held rigid and straight. However, the leg is rarely raised to a completely perpendicular position.

In more intense aggressive interactions, individuals may employ all four ambulatory legs in a quadruple raise. While all four legs are engaged in this manner, the animal maintains an upright position by using its claws for support and/or leaning back, balancing itself on its shell.

In the hermit crab world, shells are extremely valuable and important. They often fight for them.

An attacking Blue Leg Hermit Crab often moves into contact from behind and turns the other on its back. Next, it starts shaking the other crab until it cannot hold the shell. After an initial investigation, the attacker usually moves into the new shell.

It does this in such a manner that it maintains possession of both shells even after it has moved into the new one, presumably testing the fitness of the new shell. Once occupied and satisfied with the new shell, the winner releases the old one, and the losing crab moves into the old shell of the winning crab.

Important: It is very important to keep a few additional shells in the aquarium. In crowded conditions, such as are common in nature for this species, the loser is subject to almost certain death from the attacks of other crabs, fish, etc., if the winner prevents its entering a shell for more than a few seconds. A naked crab cannot protect its abdomen and can be torn to bits rapidly.

Overall, males are generally larger than females. Other than general size, there is no visible external sexual dimorphism, unless your hermit crab is willing to come rather far out of its shell.

In this case, the sex can be determined according to the presence or absence of external primary sexual traits. The female has tiny genital openings called gonopores. The gonopores are located on the fifth pair of pereopods in females and at the base of the third pair of pereopods in males.

Blue leg hermit crabs also have intersex individuals. However, they do not occur often in this species.

Mating

As in many crustaceans, Blue leg hermit crabs can successfully mate only for a short time following a female molt.

Male hermit crabs can sense when a female will be ready to molt and grasp her prior to her molting; how they do this is not known. This time may vary from a few minutes to 6 hours. The male may start violent rocking and the frequency gradually increases.

Shortly before copulation, the female molts. When the female molts, the male grabs the old exoskeleton of the female and pulls it out of the shell. By doing so, the male actually "helps" the female out of her exoskeleton by actively pulling at the legs and chelipeds. The copulation lasts only 1–3 seconds.

After copulation, the male may push the female away and mating is completed. However, in most cases, the male stays with the female and continues to do a series of violent and gentle rocking. This behavior protects the recently molted and weak female from being attacked by other shell-seeking hermit crabs. During this time, the female's exoskeleton hardens.

Breeding

It is relatively difficult to breed a Blue Leg Hermit Crab in captivity. No proof could be found that anybody has managed to breed them in aquariums. Hermit crab larvae have differing salinity needs, making them almost impossible to breed in captivity.

Even biologists know little about reproduction in this species. They do not even know what type of egg development (e.g., direct, abbreviated, indirect) it has.

The only facts known about breeding are:

  • Fecundity usually increases with female body size in hermit crabs.
  • The egg clutch varied between 200–600 embryos.

Reef safety

In most cases, Blue Leg Hermit Crabs are almost completely reef safe. This makes them some of the few good tankmates for the Beadlet Anemone (Actinia equina).

However, there are reports that aquarists had better success keeping corals alive without Blue Leg Hermit Crabs. They say that some of these crabs kept crawling on and picking at their SPS corals. Sharp feet can damage the soft flesh of the corals.

Tankmates

The Blue Leg Hermit Crab can live in peace with other aquatic animals. Although they live in a hard shell, it is advisable to take caution when keeping them with the more aggressive marine invertebrates.

For example, you can keep them with non-aggressive and relatively small fish like mollies, guppies, tetras and zebra blennies.

Try not to keep them in the same tank with snails because they can try to kill them just for their shells. Cerith snails are particularly favored by Clibanarius tricolor, so reef safe does not mean snail safe. If you provide enough empty shells in your aquarium you will avoid a lot of problems, but it will not eliminate them. If the Blue Leg Hermit Crab decides that it needs a particular shell, it can be hard to dissuade.

Avoid overstocking. These hermit crabs can become aggressive if there are too many of them in an aquarium due to competition for shells, and could become destructive if the food supply is reduced.

They can share a tank with other hermit crabs such as Halloween hermit crabs (Ciliopagurus strigatus). These species prefer different types of snail shells, so there should be no problems.

Marine shrimp like skunk cleaner shrimp, red fire shrimp, peppermint shrimp and harlequin shrimp are also good tankmates. Coral banded shrimp are not recommended together with them.

In conclusion

Blue Leg Hermit Crabs are beautiful and eye-catching in color, as well as very easy to care for. One of the greatest advantages of owning them is that they help clean whichever tank they live in, which makes them almost ideal creatures for many aquarists.
